Wool
WUUL
noun
From the Saxon wull, akin to the Latin vellus, a fleece — the soft crimped fibre shorn from the sheep, the plainest clothing of the plainest people, and in Scripture the standing figure of whiteness.

Biblical Definition

Wool is the fleece of the sheep, shorn, washed, carded, and spun. It is the poor man’s warmth and the shepherd’s wage, the first fruit of the flock and the commonest cloth in Israel. Scripture makes three great uses of it. First, it is the emblem of pardon: “though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool” (Isa 1:18). The Lord does not say the scarlet will be dulled or covered; He says it shall be as wool, which is white not by bleaching but by nature, as it comes from the beast. That is justification, not reformation. Second, wool is the emblem of the Ancient of days, whose hair is “like the pure wool” (Dan 7:9), and of the glorified Christ, whose head and hairs were white like wool (Rev 1:14) — eternity and spotless purity in one image. Third, wool is fenced by law. It may not be woven with linen in one garment (Deu 22:11), and the ministering priests of Ezekiel’s temple wear linen only, for “no wool shall come upon them” where they sweat and serve. The virtuous woman seeks wool and flax and works willingly with her hands (Pro 31:13); Gideon laid a fleece of wool upon the floor and asked a sign.

Webster 1828 Definition

The soft curled hair or fleece of sheep and like animals; in Scripture the emblem of whiteness, of pardon, and of the Ancient of days.

expand to see more

WOOL, n. [Sax. wull; L. vellus, a fleece.] That soft species of hair which grows on sheep and some other animals, remarkable for its crimped fibre, which fits it for spinning and felting.

It is distinguished from hair by its curl and its readiness to mat and take the dye.

Short, curled hair on the head, as in the phrase “hair like the pure wool” (Dan 7:9).

The Mosaic law forbade the wearing of a garment of woollen and linen together (Deu 22:11; Lev 19:19).

Wool and flax are named together as the staple materials of household industry (Pro 31:13; Hos 2:9).

Key Scripture

Isa 1:18 — "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD: though your sins be as scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they be red like crimson, they shall be as wool."

Deu 22:11 — "Thou shalt not wear a garment of divers sorts, as of woollen and linen together."

Dan 7:9 — "I beheld till the thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit, whose garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like the pure wool: his throne was like the fiery flame, and his wheels as burning fire."

Jdg 6:37 — "Behold, I will put a fleece of wool in the floor; and if the dew be on the fleece only, and it be dry upon all the earth beside, then shall I know that thou wilt save Israel by mine hand, as thou hast said."

Modern Corruption

Gideon’s fleece has been turned into a method. “Putting out a fleece” is now taught as an ordinary way to get guidance from God, and the prosperity preachers make it a lever for extracting promised returns.

expand to see more

Jdg 6:37 has been lifted out of its narrative and made a technique. Believers are taught to “put out a fleece” — to name a sign, set a condition, and read the outcome as God’s voice — and in the prosperity teaching the fleece becomes frankly transactional: a sum given, a seed sown, with a specified return demanded of God in exchange. Both misuse the text. Gideon was not seeking guidance; he had already been told plainly, twice, what the LORD would do. He was doubting a word already spoken, and he knew it, for he says, “Let not thine anger be hot against me.” God condescended to a weak and fearful man, as He often does, but condescension to weakness is not the institution of a method. Nor is the fleece a lever. The God who answered Gideon is not a mechanism to be operated by anyone who repeats the motions, and the promise attached to the modern fleece — give this, receive that — is not found in Judges or anywhere else. We are not left to signs. We have the Scriptures, the counsel of the church, the ordinary providence of God, and prayer for wisdom which He gives liberally and upbraideth not.

Recover instead what wool was chiefly given to preach. Isa 1:18 is the high use, and it is a courtroom scene, not a laundry. The LORD summons a rebellious people to reason with Him, and He does not propose that they scrub the scarlet out; He declares what He will make of it. Scarlet and crimson were the fastest dyes known — twice-dipped, deliberately permanent, the very colours chosen because they would not wash out. That is the choice of the figure: sin at its most ineradicable, set against a whiteness that is not achieved but given, the native whiteness of the fleece as it leaves the sheep. And the whiteness has a cost, for the fleece comes off a lamb. So the wool of Isa 1:18 and the Lamb of Joh 1:29 are the same doctrine: righteousness imputed, not attained; a garment received, not laundered.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The shorn fleece of the sheep — the commonest cloth in Israel and the Bible’s standing emblem of a whiteness that is given, not achieved.

expand to see more

Wool — Saxon wull; compare Latin vellus, a fleece.

Hebrew tsemer, wool; Greek erion (Heb 9:19; Rev 1:14).

Isa 1:18 sets it against scarlet and crimson — the two fastest dyes of the ancient world.

Dan 7:9 and Rev 1:14 give the same white-wool hair to the Ancient of days and to the risen Christ.

Forbidden to be mingled with linen in one garment (Deu 22:11) and excluded from the ministering priest’s dress (Eze 44:17).

Usage

"As wool, not bleached wool: Isa 1:18 promises a whiteness native to the fleece, which is imputation, not reform."

"Scarlet and crimson were chosen because they never wash out — that is the measure of the mercy."

"Gideon’s fleece was condescension to a fearful man, never a method for prying guidance out of God."
